KEY MESSAGE 1...Remnants of Hurricane Isaias to bring rain, breezy 
to windy conditions, and the threat of tornadoes Sunday.

Although the remaining circulation from Isaias is still down
across Georgia, the extent of this system extends well to the
north. While a longstanding high cirrus shield remains overhead,
some weak to modest radar returns are evident south of I-64.
While there is still low-level dry air to contend with, expect
the column to saturate in time. Otherwise, the forecast remains
on track (read below for more information).

Hurricane Isaias is forecast to move north toward the TN Valley 
today as it weakens and eventually loses all of its tropical 
characteristics. The mid-level circulation strengthens and becomes a 
large cutoff low later tonight. To the east, surface high pressure 
over the Northeast today moves offshore off southern New England 
tonight. 

The interaction of Isaias' remnants to the west and surface high to 
the east will create a large area of convergence / broad frontal 
zone over the Mid-Atlantic. There is good model agreement that rain 
steadily moves from south to north this evening into tonight as 
forcing for ascent increases with some mid-level height falls in 
response to the approaching cutoff low. It'll take a bit of time for 
the surface to truly saturate, so any rain late afternoon to this 
evening in Central Virginia is going to be light. Eventually, 
tropical moisture with PWATs at or above 2" surges in after 
midnight. 

It is worth mentioning again that conditions are favorable for a 
widespread soaking rain, and 00Z models have responded with more QPF 
across the region. Forcing for ascent increases tonight, and 
especially Sunday morning into Sunday afternoon as mid-level heights 
fall with the approach of the cutoff low. Enhanced low-level 
convergence and moisture transport will peak Sunday morning into 
early Sunday afternoon. Strengthening easterly flow into the Blue 
Ridge could also produce enhanced rain amounts due to orographic 
effects. As a result, forecast rain amounts have increased to 1.5-
2.5", with locally higher amounts of 3-4" possible. No Flood Watch 
issued with this forecast update as the heaviest rain is forecast to 
occur in areas that can handle it, but will continue to monitor the 
latest guidance today.

Another noticeable trend in the 00Z guidance is the higher 
probabilities for severe weather Sunday afternoon. The main 
synoptically forced rain moves north of the area early Sunday 
afternoon. Rapid height-falls and increasing low-level winds provide 
a few hour window where some breaks in the clouds area possible, 
leading to pockets of instability. A surface wave of low pressure 
moves right through our area Sunday afternoon. Forecast soundings 
indicate large, swooping hodographs, with ample shear in place  to 
support organized severe convection. Clusters of thunderstorms 
develop along the leading edge of the surface low pressure, with 
tornadoes and damaging wind gusts as the main threats (looks mostly 
to be east of the Blue Ridge). The NAM12, RRFS, and 06Z HRRR all 
show this scenario. The big question still remains how much 
instability actually develops. SPC has introduced a Slight Risk for 
Sunday just to our south, with a Marginal Risk north to the MD/PA 
border.

The strong mid-level circulation is going to bring windy conditions 
to the Alleghenies and Blue Ridge, starting late tonight into Sunday 
morning. Wind Advisories have been issued for downsloping easterly 
winds in the Alleghenies (western Garrett, western Grant, and 
western Pendleton Counties), and the Blue Ridge. The current 
forecast for peak wind gusts is 40-50 mph in the Alleghenies/Blue 
Ridge and 20-30 mph elsewhere.

The remnants of Isaias push offshore Monday, bringing an end to any 
lingering showers. While conditions return humid and warm Monday, 
there likely won't be much in the way of shower activity due to 
subsidence behind the departing trough.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Above normal temperatures Tuesday will fall the 
second half of the week as moisture starved fronts move through.

Brief ridging in the wake of the tropical remnants may bring high 
temperatures Tuesday to near 80 degrees. Low pressure passing north 
of the area will send a cold front southward Tuesday night. Most of 
the rain likely remains across Pennsylvania, although some showers 
may sneak southward. Showers will also be possible along the 
Allegheny Front. There's still some significant model spread on the 
progression of this front during the middle of the week, with a 
large spread of temperatures possible on Wednesday. However, the 
general trend will be downward for the second half of the week. A 
wave of low pressure or cold front may approach toward the end of 
the week which could bring some rain, but model spread remains high 
on the details.
